claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by synchronization of the reduction kinetics of all metal precursors.
Matched thermal and chemical decomposition profiles cause the precursor reduction events to occur concurrently.
Concurrent precursor reduction causes the metal atoms to nucleate simultaneously.
Simultaneous nucleation produces homogeneous alloying and a uniform atomic distribution.
Simultaneous nucleation produces nanoparticles with high surface-atom exposure or high surface area.
Even slight asynchronies in precursor reduction promote sequential nucleation.
During sequential reduction, the metals reduced first form nuclei that act as sinks for atoms released later.
Asynchronous reduction produces irregular or uncontrolled nanoparticle morphologies.
Asynchronous reduction leads to higher decomposition temperatures.
Changing heating rate, ligand environment, or atmosphere can synchronize the reduction or decomposition onset temperatures of the precursors.
The synchronized condition will yield more homogeneous elemental distributions than an otherwise identical unsynchronized baseline.
The synchronized condition will yield lower and more controlled decomposition temperatures than the unsynchronized baseline.
The hypothesis applies particularly to noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticle systems containing more than five elements and requiring high surface-atom exposure.
The hypothesis may not apply when precursor-chemistry differences make kinetic matching infeasible.
The hypothesis may not apply when subsequent thermal treatments overshadow the effects of nucleation kinetics.
The degree of synchronization required and the tolerable kinetic mismatch depend on precursor chemistry and the solvent or ligand environment.
